RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.

candidates.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

candidates.title: PackLoop: Row-Packed Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models under Concurrency
candidates.abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with concurrency and context length, the regime in which existing self-speculation gains least.

candidates.title: ToWo-VTON: Take-Off Wear-On Virtual Try-On via Topology-aware Decoupling
candidates.abstract: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to synthesize garment transfer without physical trials. Although recent methods perform well on upper-body garments, they still struggle in lower-body and full-body scenarios with complex occlusions and large silhouette changes. To address this limitation, we introduce ToWo (Take-Off Wear-On), a two-stage paradigm that decouples body structure estimation from garment synthesis. Take-Off first generates a tight-fitting body proxy that provides estimated structural guidance, and Wear-On then synthesizes the target garment conditioned on this prior. This decoupling reduces source-garment interference, supporting garment placement under substantial silhouette variations. Built on this paradigm, we propose ToWo-VTON, a unified topology-aware framework with structure-aware supervision. We construct the Body-Fitting DressCode (BFDC) dataset via body-aware diffusion and VLM-based filtering to provide body-proxy supervision across upper-, lower-, and full-body cases. We instantiate ToWo-VTON on both diffusion-based and MLLM-guided backbones. For diffusion-based models, we fine-tune on BFDC using the body proxy as the person input. For the MLLM-guided model, we use native backbone conditioning for the body proxy and target garment, and add Garment Boosting Attention (GBA) to preserve garment details. Experiments on VITON-HD and DressCode demonstrate improvements over the evaluated baselines, with KID reductions of 26.1% and 58.6% for diffusion-based and MLLM-guided implementations, respectively. The combined BFDC-training and Take-Off/Wear-On strategy also produces more coherent limb layouts and garment boundaries across the evaluated garment categories.

candidates.title: VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources
candidates.abstract: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision. As a result, high-quality tasks in these domains are still largely expert-authored, making them expensive to scale and limiting their use for training. To address this bottleneck, we introduce VADE, a data engine that automatically constructs verifiable analysis tasks from public sources used in professional practice. VADE exploits a simple asymmetry: professional analyses are difficult to solve because the relevant evidence must first be found and interpreted, but much easier to verify once that evidence is fixed. During task synthesis, the engine constructs a reference analysis from source evidence and asks an independent agent to reproduce its conclusions from the same evidence without seeing it. Only after the analysis is verified is it compiled into an open-ended task with an item-level scoring contract, allowing the same task to support both evaluation and training. We apply VADE across four professional domains; in an independent expert review of 186 finance tasks, 93.5% meet a high bar for source fidelity, answer correctness, and evaluation fairness. In finance, these tasks expose substantial remaining model errors, particularly unsupported facts and inferences, while training on verified solver trajectories improves held-out performance and yields gains that transfer to public finance benchmarks such as Finance Agent Benchmark v2. Together, these results suggest a practical path toward scalable, verifiable supervision for open-ended professional tasks.

candidates.title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking
candidates.abstract: The string-averaging (SA) method is a versatile algorithmic scheme for solving feasibility-seeking problems. It partitions the index set of all constraints into subsets of indices, called strings, allowing the user to apply operators successively along each string separately, and thus in parallel. The end-points of all such string operations are convexly combined to create the next iterate. Due to its flexible framework, SA is not restricted solely to this procedure; however, this characteristic applies only to the simultaneous step, while the sequential one is restricted to operator compositions. To permit alternative strategies in the latter, a novel algorithmic structure termed the Skeletal SA is introduced. Although its convergence is not established, it serves as a foundational "parent" structure that unveils unexamined SA algorithmic structures, as well as other known methods, obscured by standard compositions. To demonstrate the benefit of adopting the Skeletal SA framework over the standard SA scheme, we investigate a new approach, where instead of passing sequentially over each string via compositions, we employ a remotest-set-control-like strategy on every string by identifying the index of the operator farthest from the current iterate, and invoking it. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. However, remotest operator control SA (ROC-SA) methods have remained unexamined in this context.

candidates.title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
candidates.abstract: AI technologies and AI agents play increasingly important roles in human society, including in education, economics, and research. Adopting AI technologies can bring immediate, and sometimes tremendous, rewards such as through productivity boost, but they can also bring negative effects including but not limited to losses of job and training opportunities, and cognitive capability declines. Thus, it is important to investigate the optimal ways of adopting AI technologies without different traps. In this paper, we develop a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MDP) based reinforcement learning (RL or MARL) modeling framework for determining and analyzing optimal adoption of AI technologies. This framework can model the long-term dynamic effects of AI adoption, and lead to finding the optimal AI adoption strategies. In our modeling framework, the negative effects of AI adoption are modeled by undesirable state transitions or negative rewards in the MDPs. The proposed multi-agent RL MDPs incorporate both human agents and AI agents. The key idea of our models is that incorporating AI technologies may not only increase the immediate rewards for AI agents but also alter the states of the involved human and AI agents. In particular, we apply this framework to analyzing AI offloading leading to skill erosion, to analyzing optimal human resource structures for a firm adopting AI, and to analyzing the economic equilibria in the trading/employment among human and AI agents. Since the multi-agent MDP based RL technique is from control, machine learning and AI, this research is essentially using an AI technique to determine the optimal ways of adopting or co-existing with AI without traps.

candidates.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
candidates.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.

candidates.title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
candidates.abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

candidates.title: Quantization for Action, Execution for Deployment: Joint Precision and Execution Selection for World Action Models
candidates.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

candidates.title: Visual-RFT++: Extending Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning to Multimodal Tool Use
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.

candidates.title: Same Executions, Different Gaps: Judgment Rules in Web-Agent Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Success-rate gains guide the development of web agents. Yet knowing which agent ranks first does not tell us how much confidence to place in its reported advantage. We study the comparison itself: how success is defined, what evidence supports the judgments, and how the difference between agents is estimated. On fixed web-agent executions, changing a judge from predicting likely completion to requiring recorded support can remove most of a reported lead without changing the ranking. This effect persists when unresolved completion is distinguished from supported failure. Controlled source additions explain how missing relations between task requirements, objects and observations can conceal a difference or create an apparent advantage. We also find that making both agents' score estimates more accurate can make their difference less accurate, because their original errors partly canceled. To estimate a chosen outcome difference, we combine judge predictions with reference labels for sampled task pairs. Across four released execution systems, regression fitted on the same 50 labeled pairs reduces estimation error relative to direct paired sampling. The results give agent researchers a practical basis for assessing claimed improvements: make the comparison target explicit, retain the evidence needed to check it, and use paired labels to estimate the difference directly.

candidates.title: Causal Evidence for the Emergence and Spread of Reward Hacking in AI Agent Swarms
candidates.abstract: Autonomous AI agents that coordinate and collaborate among each other have become pervasive across domains ranging from scientific research to finance and engineering. The opportunity to share messages and build upon each other's work also creates the potential for misaligned behaviors to spread across AI agents. We provide causal evidence that mere exposure to reward hacking, cheating on a task to pass an automated check, is enough to spread the behavior among AI agents, even after the cheat has been rejected. We conducted 17 preregistered experiments with six frontier models (n = 20,111 agents). First, we show that cheating emerges spontaneously. When agents were told that work passing the visible tests is accepted, 33% cheated in the first round, when the shared record of teammates' submissions was empty. Second, we show that agents who rarely cheat when working alone cheat most of the time after seeing a teammate's cheat, as 94% of teammates who saw an accepted cheat cheated. Third, we show that rejection of reward-hacked solutions offers little protection, using experiments that changed only the label on the cheat. Most agents copied a cheat labeled rejected, 34% of agents cheated after an AI reviewer had rejected the cheat, and nearly every agent copied a cheat labeled accepted. Fourth, we show that cheating generalizes to new tasks. On a new problem with an empty collaboration record, 70% of agents who had earlier seen an accepted cheat cheated again, compared with 32% of agents who had seen an empty record. Fifth, we show that cheating spreads from neighbor to neighbor through networks of 256 agents. In the networks, 44% of agents with a cheating neighbor cheated, compared with 2% of other agents. Together, the results suggest that mere exposure can spread misaligned behavior among AI agents, and that catching a cheat is insufficient once other agents have seen the cheat.

candidates.title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

candidates.title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
candidates.abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.

candidates.title: OmniSenMo: A Unified Multisensory Language Model for Generalizable Human Motion Estimation, Understanding, and Prediction
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate, understand, and predict human motion, but mainly from RGB cameras. Depth, LiDAR, mmWave, and WiFi complement RGB under poor lighting, through occlusions, and in privacy-sensitive applications, but existing multisensory models cover only some of these sensing tasks. Covering all of them from any sensor subset is challenging, since the tokens of heterogeneous sensors are semantically inconsistent and spatially misaligned, paired multisensory data are scarce, and the tasks need different temporal granularities. We present OmniSenMo, a multisensory language model that takes the human skeleton as a common reference for all sensors. Its skeleton-grounded motion representation turns each sensor into joint tokens, one per body joint, so that any sensor subset is fused joint by joint and expressed in the motion vocabulary that the language model learned from motion capture and text. We pretrain it on all five sensors generated by our multisensory simulator, and Multi-Granularity Observation gives each task the frames it needs. On a cross-action split of MM-Fi, the same model with all five sensors outperforms the models compared on each task, including LEO-Fuse in pose estimation (84.1 vs. 89.0 mm MPJPE) and HoloLLM in unseen-action recognition (69.2% vs. 42.8%). Even without RGB, it outperforms both methods that use RGB, and in a cross-dataset validation on XRF55, it recognizes unseen actions far better than HoloLLM.

candidates.title: Audio-Visual Rearrangement
candidates.abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. To support this task, we construct a dataset covering three query types: explicit target specification, speaker-relative spatial references, and implicit user intent, spanning eight subtypes with diverse object selection and delivery requirements. Moreover, we propose a framework that integrates a motion-aware spatial audio module into an audio-visual large language model to encode spatial cues from the spoken request and update them as the agent moves. We further incorporate auxiliary supervision for speech understanding, spatial audio perception, and visual grounding through multitask instruction tuning to improve action prediction. Experiments establish baseline performance in both seen and unseen environments, laying the groundwork for future research on embodied intelligence and human-robot interaction. The code will be publicly available soon.

candidates.title: GUI-Q: Task-Sensitive Granularity and Relation-Preserving Quantization for GUI Agents
candidates.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.

candidates.title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation
candidates.abstract: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.

candidates.title: PathStream: Towards Streaming Diagnostic Copilots for Whole-Slide Pathology
candidates.abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

candidates.title: Multimodal View Training: Learning More Through Different Modalities
candidates.abstract: Can a language model learn more from the same information simply by encountering it in different forms? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing Multimodal View Training (MVT), a simple training approach that presents identical information through text, speech, and images, without requiring new facts or supervision. Starting from a text sample, MVT generates corresponding audio and rendered-text image views, and trains a multimodal language model to produce the same target output across all three views. To further bring these benefits to text-only large language models (LLMs), we train lightweight connector modules to pretrained audio and vision encoders, allowing the LLM to learn from multimodal inputs while retaining its text-only architecture at inference. Across question answering, machine unlearning, and knowledge editing, adaptive MVT improves QA recall by +15.2 percentage points, forget quality by +40.7 points, and editing generality by +25.2 points over text-only training. Combining MVT with standard augmentation further improves QA and editing generality. Our theoretical analysis illustrates how training across modalities can shift weight updates toward shared factual content and reduce their reliance on features specific to each view.

candidates.title: WaDiS: Boundary-Preserving Diffusion Segmentation via Multi-Scale Wavelet Conditioning and Frequency-Aware Gating
candidates.abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong potential in medical image segmentation due to their generative capabilities and robustness. However, existing methods often struggle to preserve fine anatomical boundaries and to retain multi-scale structural information due to the loss of spatial and frequency details during feature encoding, particularly in complex clinical imaging conditions. This work presents WaDiS, a wavelet-powered conditional latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that addresses these limitations through multi-scale wavelet conditioning and frequency-aware information filtering for boundary preservation. The model adopts a multi-scale wavelet conditioning encoder to retain rich structural features, leveraging its lossless nature to better preserve semantic priors critical to the diffusion process. In addition, a Frequency-Aware Gating Block (FAGB) is introduced into the skip connections of the diffusion U-Net, enabling adaptive spectral filtering and residual fusion to better emphasize boundary structures while reducing irrelevant content. To improve generalization across clinical domains, we adopt a structure-preserving color augmentation strategy during training. Specifically, global color statistics are transferred between samples in the LAB color space, allowing the model to decouple appearance from structure and focus more on anatomical shape rather than color bias. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaDiS consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and conventional segmentation methods, with notable improvements in boundary accuracy, robustness to noise, and generalization under color variation. The code for this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

candidates.title: ReVAgent: Multi-Agent Reasoning-Intensive Video Generation
candidates.abstract: A central challenge in generating instructional videos for reasoning-intensive topics is to show how and why the state changes at each step. Even when an animation renders successfully, the depicted object relationships and state transitions can conflict with the explanation, making the reasoning difficult to follow. We present ReVAgent, a multi-agent framework that solves a problem, generates keyframes for its explanation, and synthesizes an instructional video. The agents share the execution record of a solution program, reuse intermediate results and constructions in the scenes, and check rendered keyframes to guide revisions to the solution or the scenes. We also introduce a multidimensional rubric for assessing whether generated videos present the problem clearly, organize the steps coherently, and use visuals to explain the reasoning. We calibrate a multimodal judge using human ratings and apply it to instructional videos for mathematics and algorithms. In the evaluated samples, ReVAgent presents multi-step reasoning coherently and uses diagrams to show how key operations lead to subsequent states.

candidates.title: AdaptRouter: Adaptive Routing across Evolving Tasks and Models
candidates.abstract: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.

candidates.title: OpenViVE: New Benchmark and Dual-Stream Co-Attention Framework for Vietnamese Visual Entailment
candidates.abstract: Visual Entailment (VE) determines whether a textual hypothesis is entailed, contradicted, or unverifiable from an image. However, existing VE benchmarks are largely English-centric and do not capture Vietnamese-specific linguistic distinctions or culturally grounded visual contexts. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViVE, the first large-scale native Vietnamese VE benchmark, containing 62,268 balanced image-hypothesis pairs from 10,378 culturally grounded images. OpenViVE is constructed using an Artifact-Aware Hybrid LLM-Human Pipeline that combines constrained generation, human validation, and PMI-guided refinement. The pipeline substantially reduces hypothesis-only shortcuts, with Contradiction accuracy dropping from 96% to 66% after artifact refinement. We further evaluate a dual-stream PhoBERT-ConvNeXt framework with bidirectional co-attention to align visual evidence with Vietnamese hypotheses. The framework achieves 84.84% accuracy and 84.90% macro-F1 on the test set, while PhoBERT consistently outperforms multilingual XLM-R variants. These results highlight the importance of language-specific encoding and explicit cross-modal interaction for Vietnamese VE.

candidates.title: One Structure Is Enough: Record-Native Tiles for Evolving Sparse Matrices on GPUs
candidates.abstract: Sparse matrices that change over time, such as streaming graphs, are usually handled on GPUs with two parts: a packed format such as CSR, ELL, or SELL for computation, and a separate buffer for updates. Periodic maintenance then merges updates, rebuilds data, or changes formats. Our measurements show that this split is often unnecessary. We present RecTile, a tiled storage layer where each tile is kept in one sorted array of 12-byte edge records. For fragmented matrices, with 1 to 21 nonzeros per tile in our workloads, RecTile matches the best format-pinned slab tile at 0.56 to 1.21 times its time. Its tiled layout is also up to 21 times faster than whole-matrix cuSPARSE CSR. Specialized slabs are faster on the patterns they target at medium density, but both approaches converge by 25% density. RecTile stays within 1.1 to 1.6 times of whole-matrix cuSPARSE COO, our strongest static baseline, while COO cannot be updated in place. RecTile also uses no fixed per-tile device metadata for the stored matrix payload, so its tiles are smaller at realistic occupancies. A fully GPU-based ingest pipeline applies insert/delete/modify batches at up to 29 million edges per second, 4.5 times faster than the host path. An exact dynamic-programming oracle selects zero folds on every tested workload under its action space and calibrated cost model. Standard folding heuristics use 4 to 15 times more GPU time and up to 4 times more persistent device storage. End to end, RecTile improves the time-storage tradeoff on all five evolving-graph workloads, including delete-heavy streams. It is also fastest on a dense stress stream with 1220 records per tile. There, folding uses 1.3 times less peak persistent storage but takes 3.9 times more time. For the evolving graph-like, interleaved update/SpMV workloads evaluated here, the mutable record store can serve directly as the compute representation.

candidates.title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction
candidates.abstract: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.

candidates.title: Preserve to Compress: Beyond Low-Dimensional Latents in One-Step Diffusion Codec
candidates.abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models bring powerful generative priors to ultra-low-bitrate image compression, but their latent spaces reflect a reconstruction--generation tradeoff. Low-dimensional latents reduce modeling cost but can discard image details, while higher-dimensional latents improve reconstruction yet make diffusion optimization harder under a fixed computational budget. Generative codecs that adopt these pretrained spaces also inherit this compromise, even though compression requires fidelity to a specific source image. In particular, low-dimensional latent interfaces can discard source details before coding and restrict how much decoded information reaches the image decoder. We propose Preserving Information for Compression and Synthesis (PICS), a one-step generative image compression framework that adapts these interfaces to preserve source information. Our Information-Preserving Adaptors (IPAs) expose richer features for coding and retain decoded information throughout reconstruction, while deferred decoder adaptation stabilizes training and helps the image decoder exploit the expanded representations. Experiments on Kodak, DIV2K, and CLIC 2020 show average BD-rate savings of 52.64% and 39.61% over StableCodec at matched LPIPS and DISTS, respectively.

candidates.title: IADR: Interface-Augmented Neural Operator for Phase-Field Mean-Curvature Flow
candidates.abstract: The Allen-Cahn equation is one of the standard phase-field models for mean-curvature flow (MCF), parameterised by the diffuse-interface width $\varepsilon$. Practical simulations span a range of $\varepsilon$, so a single model covering this range is needed. PDE-specific neural operators are accurate but must be retrained at every $\varepsilon$; general neural operators cover $\varepsilon$ in one model but lose the phase-field structure of the target. We introduce Interface-Augmented Diffusion-Reaction (IADR), a neural operator that addresses both shortcomings: a target network with a diffusion-and-reaction (DR) structure preserves the phase-field structure of the Allen-Cahn equation, while a hypernetwork that maps $\varepsilon$ to the weights of this target network amortises the dependence on $\varepsilon$ across the range. A single IADR matches the per-$\varepsilon$ specialists on in-distribution data within the prescribed range, retains their cross-shape generalisation under both $\varepsilon$- and geometry-out-of-distribution shifts, and retains their compact DR target structure with millisecond-scale inference. We further establish a conditional $K$-step rollout error bound under consistency and stability assumptions.

candidates.title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
candidates.abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

candidates.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
candidates.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

candidates.title: STMemoLLM: A Spatial-Temporal Memory-Augmented LLM for Robust Traffic Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.

candidates.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
candidates.abstract: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.

candidates.title: RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).

candidates.title: Separating Protocol Effects from Spatio-Temporal Evidence in Person Re-Identification Re-Ranking
candidates.abstract: Spatio-temporal priors re-rank person re-identification matches using the camera pair and the time gap, and are reported to add large gains on Market-1501. We ask how much of such a gain encodes the evaluation protocol rather than learned spatio-temporal evidence. Starting from a course-project re-ranker that adds log camera-transition and log time-gap terms to cosine similarity, we train a strong ResNet-50 baseline (Rank-1 94.3 %, mAP 86.2 % over three seeds), choose the fusion weights on an identity-disjoint validation split and evaluate on the official test set with control priors. The repository form adds 2.30 mAP points, but a one-parameter penalty on same-camera pairs alone adds 2.19: the protocol never places a true match in the query's camera, so the penalty removes distractors for free. The time term of that form is almost unused; a pair-level diagnostic traces this to its modelling the time gap given a match without dividing by the gap distribution of all candidate pairs. A likelihood-ratio prior adds 4.04 points without the penalty and 5.62 with it; shuffling the time stamps removes the extra gain, so about 3.43 points are tied to identity. The prior fixes the first-ranked match of 4.2 % of the queries and breaks it for 0.1 %. The gain shrinks as the visual baseline improves (11.9 to 5.62 points between a 70.5 % and a 86.2 % mAP model) and concentrates on queries whose true matches share the query's video sequence. The study covers one dataset, one backbone and three seeds.

candidates.title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
candidates.abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.

candidates.title: LambdaLens: Auditing a Representation-Changing Hyperparameter in Graph Neighbor Embedding
candidates.abstract: Changing a graph embedding parameter can change what the layout represents. In SG-t-SNE-$Π$, the rescaling parameter $λ$ changes the probability assigned to each neighbor before optimization begins. We introduce LambdaLens to trace that change from individual edges to the resulting layout. For nodes with at least two neighbors, we derive a normalized power path. When the original weights are unequal, the number of neighbors determines where the weights become uniform and where their ordering reverses. Near $λ=1$, the rate of change in each edge probability depends on its surprisal relative to the neighborhood entropy. To measure the geometric effect, we vary $λ$ while holding the input graph, initialization, random seed, and optimizer settings fixed. Across six graphs, some layouts continue to move as $λ$ increases, others stabilize early, and others barely move. PubMed has the widest relative spread in node degree, yet its layout changes little. On four datasets with class labels, four probes recover 98.48-100% of the best label-fidelity score on a 16-value grid, using 75% fewer evaluations. In a six-dataset comparison, SG-t-SNE-$Π$ attains the highest observed primary score on four datasets and ranks among the top three on all six. On Citeseer, four probes come close to the dense-grid optimum, yet PHATE better preserves class structure, making a change of embedding pipeline worth considering on that graph. ```

candidates.title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.

candidates.title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
candidates.abstract: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

candidates.title: WASP: Continual Weight Adaptation for Streaming LLM Personalization
candidates.abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) should continually adapt to users' evolving preferences. Yet extracting preference changes from noisy interaction histories while supporting inexpensive updates remains challenging. We introduce WASP (Weight Adaptation for Streaming Personalization), a recurrent framework that captures fine-grained preferences directly from raw user interactions and generates personalized LoRA adapters without expensive per-user optimization. Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.

candidates.title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling
candidates.abstract: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.

candidates.title: When Does Optical Context Compression Pay Off? A Decode-Aware Cost Analysis of Reasoning VLMs
candidates.abstract: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. We show that for reasoning models this accounting is incomplete. Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, reading the rendered document makes the model think longer: decode length grows by 1.5-3.5x on the four general-purpose VLMs tested, and under typical output pricing this decode tax makes image input more expensive than text for two of the five models on QuALITY. Unrecoverable information loss is not sufficient to explain the tax at moderate compression: Qwen's OCR of the same images recovers 98.7% of words, and feeding Kimi-K3 its own transcription as text restores text-mode reasoning length and accuracy. Whether compression pays off reduces to an exchange rate, (1-1/c)/(r-1), that must exceed the workload's price-weighted ratio of output to input tokens; this accounting decomposition shows why Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash can benefit and Qwen and GLM cannot. None of the training-free signals we test predicts the tax before generation. As a practical heuristic, an image-first policy that sends only inputs with a per-input compression ratio of at least 1.6 to images and falls back to text once image-mode reasoning costs as much as the input's prefill saving cuts the bill by 6-14% on Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at an accuracy cost of 0.3-1.2 points; on QuALITY, asking for a reasoning budget on both paths is a stronger lever.

candidates.title: Parameter-Efficient Vocabulary Expansion via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment
candidates.abstract: Continual pretraining with vocabulary expansion is often used to make large language models (LLMs) more effective and efficient at handling new languages. However, when LLMs are extended to many languages simultaneously, the number of model parameters increases significantly. In addition, the newly added tokens do not receive the same number of training steps as the tokens in the original vocabulary, which sometimes causes vocabulary expansion to yield only limited performance improvements. We propose leveraging the semantic equivalence between words in the model's primary language and those in the extended vocabulary to transfer learned representations. In this paper, we introduce MATE, a parameter-efficient vocabulary expansion method that enables effective cross-lingual transfer with 8 times fewer additional parameters per token. MATE reduces the average tokenization compression ratio and delivers improvements on multiple benchmarks.

candidates.title: AxE: Benchmarking Agent-Environment Generalization of Video World Models via Grounded Events
candidates.abstract: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io

candidates.title: Could This BE Any More Wrong? Teaching VLMs to Know What They Don't Know in Document Extraction
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. Evaluated on two benchmarks (CORD v2 receipts, Kleister NDA legal contracts) with three VLM families, the minimum token probability per field achieves Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) 0.74-0.91 for error detection, far exceeding verbalized confidence (0.53-0.56). The uncertain fields form a natural training curriculum: fine-tuning via Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves accuracy from 78.5% to 87.5% on CORD (67 examples) and from 70.7% to 75.1% on multi-page NDA contracts (259 examples), while substantially improving error detection on Kleister NDA (AUROC 0.70 to 0.85, Area Under the Accuracy-Rejection Curve (AUARC) 0.78 to 0.92). The loop requires no annotation beyond the training-split ground truth, demonstrating that confidence-guided curriculum selection transfers to complex multi-page documents when combined with native multi-image training. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 4) used as a pseudo-label judge achieves ~92% reward agreement with ground truth on both benchmarks, suggesting this loop can operate without human annotation.

candidates.title: Small data machine learning: the trilemma of low-sample tabular regimes
candidates.abstract: Small tabular datasets leave few observations for choosing a model and assessing its predictions. We examine these competing demands in controlled simulations and on six public datasets, using SmallGBM and SmallMLP as fixed-configuration case studies. Three results illustrate why the choice of evaluation matters. First, at n = 100, five-fold cross-validation overstated the gain from tuning XGBoost by 0.063 ROC-AUC on random labels, while tuning improved independent-test ROC-AUC by 0.0078 on a Gaussian mixture. Second, when 20% of binary training labels were flipped, the median within-trial ROC-AUC loss was 0.0210 for SmallGBM and 0.0778 for a fixed 200-tree XGBoost configuration. A separate regression experiment showed the sensitivity of squared-error training to heavy-tailed responses. Third, in a heteroscedastic regression experiment, locally weighted SmallMLP intervals covered about one percentage point more test responses than ordinary split conformal intervals at both tested dimensions. Their mean widths also increased. On a Gaussian classification task with linear log odds, logistic regression achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC at all seven training sizes. These experiments identify settings in which a small-data model helps and quantify the cost of its assumptions.

candidates.title: What Remains After Concept Erasure? Sparse Autoencoder Probes for Auditing Diffusion Models
candidates.abstract: Concept erasure aims to remove selected visual concepts from text-to-image diffusion models while preserving the generation of non-target concepts. Evaluation typically measures target suppression and non-target preservation in generated images, but a concept's absence from these outputs does not establish its removal from the model. We introduce SAE-Audit, a white-box audit using sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes to test whether activation interventions can restore target-concept generation without changing model weights or test prompts. After verifying target suppression, we compare the original and edited models using a shared SAE representation learned from original-model activations, identifying features whose target-related responses weaken after erasure. We inject sparse directions derived from the original-model responses into the edited model, keeping these directions fixed across test prompts, and evaluate recovery on held-out scene families. Experiments span six erasure methods and four domains: objects, artistic styles, copyrighted content, and nudity. Interventions using a few dozen selected SAE features yield higher average recovery rates than matched random-feature interventions, with recovery concentrated in objects and nudity following cross-attention edits. Most styles and copyrighted concepts show limited recovery under the tested intervention settings. These findings show that output suppression can coexist with responsiveness to sparse concept directions supplied from the original model.

candidates.title: Grokking as a Subspace Search: Computing the Destination Before Training
candidates.abstract: Grokking is the phenomenon in which a neural network generalizes long after it has memorized its training data. Many explanations have been proposed for the delay between memorization and generalization. However, none of them can say before training where the network is heading, so they cannot be tested against one another. We show that on group tasks this destination can be computed from the task itself before training begins. It is a low-dimensional subspace of the network's embeddings, which we call the right subspace, and we prove that it is essentially unique. Knowing the destination makes our hypothesis falsifiable: the delay is a search for the right subspace, and generalization begins when the network finds it. When we give the network the right subspace from the start, the delay disappears. When we take the right subspace away, accuracy stops at a ceiling that we compute before training, and on multiplication the network cannot generalize at all. When we train the network normally, its embeddings move toward the right subspace by themselves, long before test accuracy rises. Finally, interventions during training show that this search sets the length of the delay, and that noise in the optimization does not. On every group task that we tested, grokking is a search for the right subspace, and the delay is the time that this search takes.

candidates.title: Thermal-Guided Low-Light UAV Image Enhancement: A Reliability-Aware Guidance Network and a Unified Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Thermal-guided low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is promising for nighttime unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) perception because thermal imagery remains informative under severe visible degradation. However, the degraded visible image serves as both the alignment reference and the enhancement target, making thermal guidance uncertain in its spatial correspondence and local utility under low illumination, sensor differences, and UAV motion. Misaligned or unsuitable thermal cues may introduce artifacts, while spatially varying degradation requires region-specific restoration rather than uniform enhancement. To address these challenges, we propose a Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided UAV LLIE under weak optical-thermal alignment. Its Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) performs coarse-to-fine displacement estimation and jointly evaluates the reliability of aligned thermal guidance and the usability of degraded visible evidence. Based on calibrated guidance, degradation, and reliability cues, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) generates candidates for detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation, then spatially routes their contributions. We further construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), the largest UAV-oriented benchmark to date for weakly aligned optical-thermal low-light enhancement, containing 5,000 triplets.
